title: What the Fire Doesn't Take
logline: After a death in a village, volunteers from the local funeral-aid society take over the practical work of the house and yard, so the family can sit with their loss.
human_question: Once someone has died, whose job is what remains of their body?

premise.story: The hours and days after a death, told through the volunteers who quietly take over the practical work while the family grieves, with the family's full consent.
premise.place: A village home and its neighbourhood, organised by a local funeral-aid society (marana adahara samithiya).
premise.experience: White flags going up, borrowed chairs, tea made in bulk, a collection book passed around, and a family sitting apart from all of it while neighbours do the work.

concept_links.why: The source describes death as a sequence of stoppings: kamma-born matter stops first, mind-born and food-born matter fade soon after, and only temperature-born matter continues in the body afterward. What is left is not being renewed from within, only weathered, which is exactly the work the volunteers step in to care for.
The wider inventory of matter, with nothing in it called 'owner', frames why a body needs the care of others once its own life is no longer sustaining it.

what_camera_could_observe: White flags going up along the lane
Chairs borrowed, tea made in bulk for visitors
The society's collection book and record of who helped
Neighbours doing practical work: cooking, seating, arrangements
The family sitting with their loss while the household runs around them
what_must_be_real: Full family consent at every stage. The deceased must never be filmed without explicit permission, and mourning must never be staged, prolonged or repeated for the camera.

possible_arc.opening: News of a death reaching the neighbourhood.
possible_arc.turn: The house filling with practical helpers.
possible_arc.ending_open: Whatever the family and the day actually bring.

position_hint: closing candidate: a direct, unsentimental answer to what remains of a body once life has left it, and a fitting film to close the group before it hands off to the next stage

requirements: A village funeral-aid society willing to be filmed carrying out its ordinary work
A grieving family giving full, explicit, ongoing consent
Sensitivity and flexibility in scheduling around an actual death, not a staged one

suggestions.name: A village funeral-aid society (marana adahara samithiya)
suggestions.why: Village funeral-aid societies are a widespread, well-documented institution across rural Sri Lanka; Uva is suggested for geographic variety within the group.
suggestions.verify: A specific society, family and willingness to be filmed are all unverified and cannot be arranged in advance of a real death.

risks: Requires clear, explicit family consent at every single stage
Never film the deceased without explicit permission
Must not turn mourning into spectacle
drop_if: A family unwilling to be filmed at such a time
A society unwilling to participate, or no genuine access without intrusion

connections.note: One family answers 'what remains' in the days right after a death; the other watches two bodies answer the same question across a whole year.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed. Everything above is a research direction.
